title: Fidel Castro: Today He Would Have Turned 100; International Delegates Highlight His Legacy and Stand in Solidarity with Cuba
author: Luis Hernández Navarro
content:
_This article by Luis Hernández Navarro originally appeared in the[August 12,
2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/08/12/mundo/cien-anos-de-
fidel-castro-delegados-internacionales-destacan-legado-y-se-solidarizan-con-
cuba), Mexico's premier left-wing daily newspaper._

**Havana**. The Palace of Conventions looks like an anthill. Hundreds of
delegates roam its hallways and rooms, take keepsake photos, hurriedly drink
coffee, chat and, above all, fill the halls. They are gathering around the 100
years since the birth of Fidel Castro. They review his role as revolutionary
and statesman, as a driving force of health diplomacy and a popular educator,
as a central actor in the struggle against colonialism and a promoter of
sport. But today, amid this immensity of activities, the forum of solidarity
with Cuba, chaired by Miguel Díaz-Canel, stands out. In the string of
speeches, those who take the floor agree that the comandante's action remade
the world map. His bold moves on the chessboard of international relations
redrew the borders of Africa and Southeast Asia.

![International delegates gather at the Palace of Conventions in
Havana](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/fidel-castro-
centenary-02-hall.jpg)During the conferences yesterday at the Palace of
Conventions in the Cuban capital, all agreed that with his bold moves the
comandante remade the world map. Photo: Alex Castro

Although he was born in New Zealand, Michael Lapsley is honorary president of
the friendship society between South Africa (where he moved to live in 1973)
and the island. He is an Anglican priest. He directs the Institute for Healing
of Memories. He militated in the African National Congress and was expelled
from South Africa in 1976. A letter bomb sent to him by the apartheid regime
made him lose both hands and one eye. On 10 occasions he visited the Cuban
hero Gerardo Hernández in the prison where he was held in the United States.
Love, Father Lapsley says, is not only a matter of sharing emotions, but of
practical support. And he recalls that, when he had just suffered the
terrorist attack that left him without hands and with one eye, the second
person to visit him in the hospital was Cuba's ambassador. He offered him
medical treatment on the island. "Fidel Castro's legacy," he stressed, "is
that he inspires us to keep fighting for justice. No to the genocide against
Cuba!"

In his turn, the vice president of the Vietnam-Cuba friendship association
denounced that "the blockade applied against the noble people of the island is
a genocide in the 21st century." He also recalled that the bond uniting the
two sister nations transcends generations. Indeed it does. In homage to the
epic of the Vietnamese war of liberation, in the song _Madre_ (Mother),
composed in 1972, Silvio Rodríguez says: "Mother, on your day / Motherland and
mother revolution, / Mother, on your day / your boys sweep mines in Haiphong."
Right around those dates, the United States escalated its attacks against that
Asian nation with greater belligerence and cruelty. Without further preamble,
on May 1, Fidel Castro announced in the Plaza de la Revolución the dispatch of
three medical teams to Vietnam. Amid the bombing, the island's doctors devoted
themselves to saving lives and healing the wounded.

### A Vietnamese Publication as a Gesture of Reciprocity

As a small great gesture of reciprocity, Vietnam has just published in print,
together with the Cubans, the _Selected Works_ of Fidel Castro, which were
formally presented today at the Colloquium. Vietnam's National Political
Publishing House La Verdad printed 3,000 copies of the _Selected Works_ of
Fidel Castro Ruz. Vu Trong Lam was the director and editor in chief. They are
24 splendidly produced volumes, in the style of the classic selected works
that former socialist countries published with the writings of Marx, Lenin,
Mao Tse-Tung and so many other Marxist thinkers. Volume 23 consists of part of
the letters that the comandante exchanged with Hugo Chávez.

![The 23 volumes of the Selected Works of Fidel Castro on
display](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/fidel-castro-
centenary-volumes-jpg.jpg)The Fidel Castro Center presents the 23 volumes of
the Selected Works of Commander in Chief Fidel Castro on the occasion of the
centenary of his birth. Photo: Luis Hernández Navarro

Alfonso Ramón Naranjo is a retired journalist, lives in Las Tunas, in eastern
Cuba, and devotes himself to studying the Cuban War of Independence and the
combative internationalist missions in Africa, particularly in Angola. The
current crisis, caused by the new tightening of the blockade's screws, has led
him to lose significant weight. Sometimes his money is not enough, but he
assures: "we are going to survive, we are going to keep moving forward. We
have already shown it on several occasions. We did so during the Special
Period, which was very hard, though not at the levels we have reached today."

Alfonso presented a paper on Fidel as a military strategist during the war in
Angola. As he explains, the comandante had an enormous capacity to predict
what was going to happen. Reviewing declassified military documents, he found,
for example, a warning to a Cuban commander in Africa telling him that the
enemy was going to attack at a precise hour. And, indeed, at that hour the
offensive against him took place. Naranjo was in Angola in the 1975-76 period.
He returned in '77 and in '88, with Cuito Cuanavale. First he went as a war
correspondent, but he had to trade the pen for arms, to follow the troops.
When it was officially said that Cuba was collaborating with Angola, the
journalistic work began to come out. The other times he went as a combatant.
He was an officer.

In an interview with _La Jornada_ he recounts: "there is an anecdote about
Marshal Grechko, defense minister of the Soviet Union. Fidel went to a
congress of the CPSU, and, in the free moments he had at the Protocol House,
he would invite personalities to explain the development of the war in Angola
(which had begun in 1975, with the entry of the South Africans, and ended in
1990). To Grechko he detailed what the situation on the ground was like, the
trees, the soil, the rains and the rivers. Grechko stared at him and said:
'Fidel, how bad Soviet intelligence is! We never knew you had been in Angola!'
And the commander in chief answered him: no, I have not been in Angola. It is
a matter of liaison."

Every day, Castro had the information about what was going to happen. From
those reports and the photos, he came to know Angola perfectly. He issued
orders: place a tank or an anti-aircraft artillery battery at a certain point.
He predicted when the Cuban troops were going to be attacked. It was not
witchcraft, it was his intuition. He was a strategist.

![Fidel Castro cutting sugarcane in a Cuban field, October
1962](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/fidel-castro-
centenary-03-sugarcane.jpg)Fidel Castro (1926-2016) cutting sugarcane in a
Cuban field, in October 1962. Photo: AFP

"On that mission, 2,000 Cubans fell. Sometimes one man became three. We Cubans
have the desire to defend the sovereignty of the people. The Cuban, wherever
he is, has a great sense of belonging to his homeland. And we defended Angola
as if we were in Cuba. We were all completely volunteers. We only brought back
the bones of our dead," he explains.

Among the things that have been clearly established at the colloquium is that,
for Fidel Castro, the word dignity had a synonym: Palestine. In many ways and
at different moments, the speakers mentioned the comandante's role in
defending its cause and making it visible. Iraklis Tsavdaridis, executive
secretary of the World Peace Council, was no exception. Among Comandante
Castro's legacy, he said, is support for the struggle against the genocide
against the Palestinian people.

In 1966 — it was recalled at various panels — when the Organization of
Solidarity with the Peoples of Africa, Asia and Latin America was created,
Fidel promoted the recognition of the Palestinian struggle as a central link
in the fight against colonialism. In 1973, Cuba broke off diplomatic relations
with Israel and recognized the Palestine Liberation Organization as the
legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. Anticipating what we have
lived through, six years later he framed that issue as "the core of the Middle
East problem." In 1982, he received 500 Palestinian children on the island to
study.

### Foreign Minister Refutes New York Times Report

In the framework of the event, Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez refuted on
social media a slanderous report by _The New York Times_. He warned that there
is no "link or any participation by the Cuban government in human trafficking
operations in Central America or Mexico." On the contrary, he pointed out
that, in bilateral meetings with the United States, his government has warned
about the existence of operations trafficking Cubans into the United States,
whose coordinating center is in southern Florida.

Years ago, don Pablo González Casanova affirmed what has been repeated in many
ways during these three days of the colloquium: in Cuba lives a people whose
consciousness has become will, its will intelligence, and its intelligence
organization. Almost to conclude the massive solidarity event, Norberto
Galiotti, coordinator of the Latin American and Caribbean Continental Network
of Solidarity with Cuba and Just Causes, called for redoubling support for the
island. "A single drop is little," he said, "but with another, it makes a
downpour." He quoted the great Turkish poet Nazim Hikmet: "If I do not burn; /
if you do not burn, / if we do not burn, / how will the darkness / become /
light." And he called on everyone to burn in order to illuminate these dark
times.
